en.title: Production Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What production engineering covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What production engineering is
sections.text:
Production engineering is the branch of engineering that turns designs into finished goods. It decides which process makes a part, in what order, on what machine, with what tooling, at what cost and to what quality. It also designs the system around the process: the layout, the people, the schedules and the checks.

It sits between mechanical engineering, which supplies much of the science, and industrial engineering, which supplies the study of systems. A production engineer may choose a casting instead of a forging, set a cutting speed, plan a factory floor, or trace why a batch failed inspection.

Much of a product’s cost and quality is fixed by the process chosen, not by the drawing alone. These summaries teach principles. They do not replace national standards, design codes or a registered engineer. Codes and registration rules differ by country and change over time, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text:
Length, award and title differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria a BEng usually takes five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnic students commonly take an ND, then supervised industrial work, then an HND. In most of the UK a BEng usually takes three years and an MEng four, with Scotland usually a year longer. Other countries have their own patterns.

Early years are shared with other engineering students: mathematics, mechanics, materials, drawing, thermodynamics and electrical fundamentals. Middle years carry the manufacturing processes and the management subjects. The final year usually adds a project, and often workshop or plant visits.

A master’s degree adds advanced processes, modelling and simulation, smart manufacturing and research methods, ending in a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
First come the tools: engineering mathematics, an introduction to manufacturing systems, engineering drawing and CAD, materials science, statics, strength of materials, thermodynamics and fluid mechanics, and electrical fundamentals.

Next come the shaping processes. Casting pours liquid metal into a mould. Bulk deformation shapes solid metal by rolling, forging, extrusion or drawing. Sheet metal forming bends and stretches flat material. Machining cuts material away with a tool, and abrasive and non-traditional processes finish or cut hard materials. Joining and assembly put parts together, and polymer, composite and additive manufacturing cover plastics and layer-by-layer building.

Then come measurement and control: metrology, tolerances and surface finish; production planning and control; work study and ergonomics; quality management and statistical process control; lean manufacturing and just-in-time; automation, robotics and CNC; CAD/CAM and computer-integrated manufacturing; maintenance and reliability; engineering economy and cost estimation; industrial safety and environmental management; and professional practice, ethics and regulation.

At master’s level the focus moves to advanced and precision processes, modelling and simulation of manufacturing systems, Industry 4.0, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Work through each process by asking four questions: what shape can it make, what material suits it, what defects does it produce, and what does it cost per part? A sketch of the tool and workpiece answers the first question better than a paragraph.

Do the calculations by hand. For a casting, check the volume and the solidification time. For machining, check the cutting speed and the material removal rate. For a cost estimate, separate fixed from variable cost. Write units on every line and ask whether the answer is plausible.

Learn the vocabulary precisely, because terms such as tolerance, allowance and accuracy are not interchangeable. Visit a workshop if you can. Software such as CAD, CAM and simulation is useful, but learn the hand method first and check the output against a simple calculation.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for production engineers
en.short: Calculus, matrices, probability and numerical methods for production data.

sections.heading: Functions and calculus
sections.text:
A function maps each input to one output; f(x)=2x+3 is linear. The derivative f′(x) is the instantaneous rate of change, and the definite integral is the accumulated area under a curve. In production, derivatives give marginal cost, speed or cooling rate; integrals give totals from rates. To optimise, solve f′(x)=0 and check the second derivative.

Example: cost C(q)=q²+4q+100. Marginal cost is C′(q)=2q+4, so at q=10 it is 24 per unit. The extra cost from q=0 to q=10 is ∫(2q+4)dq from 0 to 10 = [q²+4q] from 0 to 10 = 140, which equals C(10)−C(0).

sections.heading: Matrices and systems
sections.text: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. A linear system can be written Ax=b, where A holds coefficients, x the unknowns and b the constants. Solve small systems by Gaussian elimination, which removes unknowns row by row; use the inverse A⁻¹ only when A is square and invertible. Matrix multiplication is defined only when columns of the first equal rows of the second. Such systems model material balances, machine loads and product mixes.

sections.heading: Probability and statistics
sections.text: Probability measures chance from 0 to 1. The mean is the average, the variance is the average squared deviation from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root, in the same units as the data. Use a sample to estimate a population, and report the sample size. A histogram shows the shape of production data; the normal distribution is a common model for variation around a target.

sections.heading: Numerical methods
sections.text: Numerical methods find answers when algebra is difficult. Bisection solves f(x)=0 by halving an interval where f changes sign. Newton-Raphson uses xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ) ÷ f′(xₙ) and converges fast near a root. The trapezium rule estimates an integral from tabulated values. For production data, plot first, then calculate averages and spread; do not fit a trend without checking the scatter.

keyPoints: A derivative is a rate of change; a definite integral is accumulated area; set f′(x)=0 for stationary points.
Solve Ax=b by Gaussian elimination; A⁻¹ exists only for a square invertible A.
Probability lies between 0 and 1; standard deviation is √variance and uses the same units as the data.
Bisection needs a sign change; Newton-Raphson uses xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ) ÷ f′(xₙ).
The trapezium rule approximates ∫f(x)dx by (h÷2)[f₀+2f₁+...+2fₙ₋₁+fₙ].

en.title: Introduction to production engineering and manufacturing systems
en.short: The scope of production engineering, production types, system inputs and outputs, and a brief history.

sections.heading: Scope and system
sections.text:
Production engineering designs, runs and improves the systems that make goods. It overlaps with mechanical, industrial, materials and electrical engineering. Its concern is the whole system: machines, methods, materials, people and information working together to turn inputs into outputs at the required quality and cost.

A production system takes inputs such as materials, energy, labour, machines and capital, and transforms them through a process into outputs: products, services, waste and information. Feedback from inspection and cost records adjusts the process. Four linked roles are the process, the method of transformation; the product, what is made; people, who operate, plan and improve; and information, which carries designs, schedules, measurements and instructions.

sections.heading: Types of production
sections.text:
Production is classified by volume and variety. Job production makes one or a few custom items, such as a bridge or tailored garment; it is flexible but costly per unit. Batch production makes a set quantity, then switches product; a bakery is an example. Mass production makes standard items in large numbers on flow lines, as with cars. Continuous production runs without stopping, as in cement or petroleum refining. Higher volume usually lowers unit cost but reduces flexibility.

Example: a furniture workshop in Kano, Nigeria, makes 20 identical chairs as one batch. If each chair needs 3 labour hours at ₦2,000 per hour, direct labour cost is 20 × 3 × 2,000 = ₦120,000. It is batch production because the workshop changes to tables afterwards.

sections.heading: History and profession
sections.text:
Manufacturing moved from craft production by artisans, through the Industrial Revolution in Britain in the eighteenth century, to mass production, numerical control, automation and computer-based planning. These changes shifted production engineering towards measurement, standardisation and system design.

Design codes, standards and professional registration differ between countries. For example, COREN regulates engineering registration in Nigeria. Check the current national code and regulator rather than assuming another country’s rules apply.

keyPoints: Production engineering designs, runs and improves systems that turn inputs into outputs.
A production system combines process, product, people and information.
Job production is custom and flexible; batch repeats a set quantity; mass and continuous production serve high volume.
Higher volume usually lowers unit cost but reduces flexibility.
Manufacturing developed from craft work through the Industrial Revolution to automation and computer-based planning.
Design codes, standards and professional registration differ by country; for example, COREN regulates engineering in Nigeria.

en.title: Engineering drawing, orthographic projection and CAD
en.short: Orthographic and isometric views, sections, dimensions, conventions and basic CAD modelling.

sections.heading: Views and projection
sections.text:
Orthographic projection shows an object by parallel views onto planes at right angles, usually front, top and side. Each view gives true shape and size for surfaces parallel to that plane. First-angle and third-angle layouts place the views differently; the projection symbol states which is used. Standards differ by country and company, so check the edition your school or employer requires.

Isometric projection shows three axes 120° apart. In an isometric drawing, lines along the axes are drawn at true length. In a true isometric projection they are shortened by √(2/3) ≈ 0.8165. Example: a 40 mm cube edge is drawn 40 mm in an isometric drawing, but 40 × 0.8165 = 32.66 mm in isometric projection.

sections.heading: Sections and dimensions
sections.text:
A section view cuts away part of the object to show internal shape. A cutting plane line marks where the cut is taken; the exposed cut surface is hatched with thin lines, usually at 45°, and adjacent parts get different hatch spacing. Hidden lines are normally left out of a section.

Dimensioning gives size and position. Use extension lines from the feature, dimension lines with arrowheads, and numerals. Give each dimension once, place it where it is easy to read, and state the unit in the title block or note. Drawings normally use millimetres unless another unit is stated. Follow the standard named on the drawing.

sections.heading: Reading drawings
sections.text: To read a drawing, identify the views, projection symbol, scale, title block and notes. Match features between views: a hole is a circle in one view and hidden lines in another. Check dimensions against the views rather than scaling the paper.

sections.heading: CAD modelling
sections.text: CAD replaces the drawing board but not the conventions. 2D CAD sketches use lines, arcs and constraints; dimensions drive geometry in parametric systems. A 3D model can be wireframe, surface or solid. Solid models use features such as extrude and revolve, then assemblies generate orthographic drawings. Layers, line types and title blocks keep output standard.

keyPoints: Orthographic views are parallel projections onto planes at right angles; first-angle and third-angle layouts differ and the symbol shows which is used.
In an isometric drawing, lines along the three axes are drawn at true length; true isometric projection shortens them by about 0.8165.
Section views use a cutting plane and hatching to show internal features; hidden lines are usually omitted.
Dimension each feature once, in millimetres unless stated otherwise, and follow the named drawing standard.
CAD 2D sketches use constraints and dimensions; 3D models may be wireframe, surface or solid and can generate drawings.
Drawing standards and professional registration differ by country; check the current official or employer standard.

en.title: Materials science for production engineers
en.short: Covers atomic and crystal structure, properties, processing and how material choice shapes manufacturing.

sections.heading: Atoms and crystals
sections.text:
Materials are built from atoms held by bonds. Metals have metallic bonds: positive ions in a sea of electrons, explaining electrical conduction and ductility. Ceramics have ionic or covalent bonds, so they are stiff and brittle. Polymers are long chain molecules with covalent bonds along the chain and weak forces between chains, so many soften on heating.

In solids, atoms often form crystals: repeating arrangements. Common metal structures are body-centred cubic (BCC), face-centred cubic (FCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP). Real crystals contain grains and defects such as vacancies and dislocations. Dislocations are line defects; their movement allows plastic deformation.

sections.heading: Properties and test
sections.text:
Mechanical properties describe response to force: strength (stress at yield or fracture), stiffness (elastic modulus), ductility (strain before fracture), hardness (resistance to indentation or scratching) and toughness (fracture resistance). Physical properties include density, melting point and conductivity; corrosion resistance is a chemical property. A stress-strain test gives modulus as stress ÷ strain in the elastic region.

For a composite, density can be estimated by the rule of mixtures: ρ = fρf + (1−f)ρm, where f is fibre volume fraction. Example: 60% glass fibre by volume (2.5 g/cm³) in epoxy (1.2 g/cm³): ρ = 0.6×2.5 + 0.4×1.2 = 1.5 + 0.48 = 1.98 g/cm³.

sections.heading: Processing and structure
sections.text:
Processing changes structure; structure sets properties. Cold working a metal increases dislocation density, raising strength but lowering ductility; annealing lets new grains form and restores ductility.

In polymers, rapid cooling can leave more amorphous (non-crystalline) material, while slow cooling can raise crystallinity, affecting stiffness and clarity. Ceramics are shaped then sintered (heated so pressed powder particles bond without melting); porosity lowers strength. In composites, fibre direction gives strength along the fibres.

sections.heading: Choosing material and process
sections.text:
Material selection and process choice are linked. A material must meet function, limits, cost and availability, and it must be manufacturable.

Brittle ceramics are not easily rolled or machined; cast irons are cast rather than rolled; thermoplastics suit injection moulding; composites suit lay-up. In a workshop, choosing high-density polyethylene (HDPE) instead of galvanised steel changes the process from welding to rotational moulding or hot-gas welding. Check standards and costs.

keyPoints: Metals have metallic bonds and crystal structures such as BCC, FCC and HCP; dislocations allow plastic deformation.
Mechanical properties include strength, stiffness, ductility, hardness and toughness; physical properties include density and conductivity.
Structure, property and processing are linked: cold work raises strength and lowers ductility, while annealing restores ductility.
Polymer crystallinity and composite fibre direction strongly affect stiffness and strength.
Composite density by the rule of mixtures is ρ = fρf + (1 − f)ρm.
Material selection must consider function, limits, cost, availability and manufacturability, which affects process choice.

en.title: Engineering mechanics: statics
en.short: Force systems, moments, equilibrium, trusses, friction and centroids for production equipment.

sections.heading: Forces and moments
sections.text:
A force is a push or pull with magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. A force system is a set of forces on a body.

Its moment about a point is M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action. A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces; its moment is F × d between them. Machine brackets and frames feel both force and moment.

sections.heading: Equilibrium
sections.text:
A particle is in equilibrium when ΣF = 0, so ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0. A rigid body is in equilibrium when ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0.

Draw a free-body diagram: the body alone with applied forces and support reactions. A pin gives two reaction components, a roller one normal reaction, a fixed support two forces and a moment.

Example: a 4 m simply supported beam carries 10 kN at 1 m from the left. Moments about the left end: R_right × 4 = 10 × 1, so R_right = 2.5 kN. Then ΣFy = 0 gives R_left = 7.5 kN. Design codes and safety factors vary by country.

sections.heading: Trusses and friction
sections.text:
A truss is a frame of straight members joined at their ends. Simple analysis assumes pin joints, loads only at joints and negligible member weight, so each member carries force only at its two ends (a two-force member). Use the method of joints or sections.

Friction opposes sliding; limiting friction is F = μN, where μ is the coefficient of friction and N is the normal force. A 200 N block with μ = 0.3 needs 60 N to start moving.

sections.heading: Centroids
sections.text:
The centroid is the geometric centre of an area. For a composite area, x̄ = Σ(A_i x_i) ÷ ΣA_i and ȳ = Σ(A_i y_i) ÷ ΣA_i.

These values locate the line of action of the weight and help find reactions on machine beds and structural sections.

keyPoints: Force is a vector; its moment about a point is M = F × d, where d is perpendicular to the line of action.
A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces and has moment F × d.
Particle equilibrium needs ΣF = 0; rigid body equilibrium needs ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0.
Under the usual assumptions, truss members are two-force members.
Limiting friction is F = μN.
For a composite area, x̄ = Σ(A_i x_i) ÷ ΣA_i and ȳ = Σ(A_i y_i) ÷ ΣA_i.

en.title: Strength of materials for production
en.short: Axial, torsion and bending stress, shear and moment, deflection, thermal stress, yield and fatigue.

sections.heading: Axial and torsion
sections.text:
Stress is force per area, σ = F ÷ A. Strain is fractional length change, ε = ΔL ÷ L. In the elastic range, σ = Eε, where E is Young’s modulus.

For a circular shaft in torsion, shear stress is τ = T r ÷ J, where T is torque, r is radial distance and J is polar second moment of area. Twist is θ = T L ÷ (G J), with G the shear modulus.

sections.heading: Bending and shear
sections.text:
Bending gives normal stress: M ÷ I = σ ÷ y = E ÷ R, where M is bending moment, I is second moment of area, y is distance from the neutral axis and R is radius of curvature.

Shear force V and bending moment M come from equilibrium and are drawn as diagrams. Beam shear stress is τ = VQ ÷ (I b), where Q is first moment of area beyond the level and b is width.

sections.heading: Deflection and heat
sections.text:
Deflection follows EI d²y/dx² = M, where EI is flexural rigidity. For a simply supported beam with a uniform load w per unit length over span L, mid-span deflection is δ = 5wL⁴ ÷ (384EI).

A free bar heated by ΔT strains by αΔT, where α is the thermal expansion coefficient. If expansion is fully prevented, thermal stress magnitude is EαΔT.

sections.heading: Failure and example
sections.text:
Yielding begins permanent deformation; yield criteria such as von Mises or Tresca compare complex stress with tensile yield strength. Fatigue is failure under repeated stress, often below yield, assessed by S-N curves, endurance limits and stress concentration. Codes and safety factors differ by country, so check the local standard.

Example: a 20 mm steel tie bar carries 50 kN. A = π × 20² ÷ 4 = 314.16 mm². σ = 50,000 ÷ 314.16 = 159.15 N/mm². With E = 200,000 N/mm², ε = 0.000796 and elongation over 1.5 m is 1.19 mm. These ideas size shafts, bolts, press frames and tooling.

keyPoints: Axial stress is σ = F ÷ A and elastic strain is ε = σ ÷ E.
For a circular shaft, torsion shear stress is τ = T r ÷ J and twist is θ = T L ÷ (G J).
Bending stress follows M ÷ I = σ ÷ y = E ÷ R.
Beam shear stress is τ = VQ ÷ (I b), and deflection follows EI d²y/dx² = M.
Fully restrained thermal stress has magnitude EαΔT.
Yield criteria and fatigue checks use factors of safety that vary by country and code.

en.title: Thermodynamics and fluid mechanics fundamentals
en.short: Energy, first law, gas and liquid properties, fluid statics, pipe flow and fluid power.

sections.heading: Energy, heat and work
sections.text:
Energy is the capacity to cause change. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; work is energy transferred by a force moving through a distance. Both are measured in joules. The first law for a closed system is Q − W = ΔU: heat added Q minus work done by the system W equals the rise in internal energy ΔU, the energy stored in the substance’s molecules.

Example: a gas absorbs 500 J and does 200 J of work, so ΔU = 500 − 200 = 300 J.

sections.heading: Gases and liquids
sections.text: A gas fills its container; a liquid keeps a nearly fixed volume and forms a free surface. For an ideal gas, pV = nRT, where p is absolute pressure, not gauge pressure, V volume, n amount in moles, R the molar gas constant and T absolute temperature in kelvin. Liquids are usually treated as incompressible, so density ρ is constant. Heating and cooling use Q = mcΔT for mass m and specific heat c.

sections.heading: Fluid statics and pipe flow
sections.text:
Fluid statics deals with fluids at rest. Pressure is p = F/A. In a static liquid, p = p₀ + ρgh, where p₀ is the pressure at the surface, h is depth below the surface and g is gravitational acceleration.

For pipe flow, continuity gives Q = A v, where Q is volume flow rate, A area and v mean velocity. Example: a 50 mm diameter pipe carries water at 2 m/s. A = π × 0.025² = 0.001963 m²; Q = 0.001963 × 2 = 0.00393 m³/s, about 3.93 litres per second. Friction causes pressure loss.

sections.heading: Fluid power components
sections.text: Fluid power uses pressurised liquid (hydraulics) or gas (pneumatics) to transmit force and motion. A pump moves liquid; a compressor supplies air. Valves control direction, pressure or flow. A cylinder converts pressure into linear force, F = pA; a motor converts flow into rotation. Filters clean the fluid, accumulators store hydraulic energy, and regulators and lubricators condition air. Hydraulics suit high force and precise control; pneumatics suit fast, clean, low-cost motion. They drive presses and clamps.

keyPoints: First law for a closed system: Q − W = ΔU, with a consistent sign convention.
Ideal gas: pV = nRT, using absolute pressure and temperature in kelvin.
Sensible heat: Q = mcΔT when no phase change occurs.
Static liquid pressure: p = p₀ + ρgh.
Continuity for pipe flow: Q = A v.
Fluid power cylinder force: F = pA; hydraulics suit high force, pneumatics fast low-cost motion.

en.title: Electrical and electronic fundamentals for production machines
en.short: DC and AC circuits, power, transformers, motors, sensors, switches and control for production.

sections.heading: Direct current
sections.text:
Direct current (DC) flows in one direction. In a simple resistive circuit, Ohm’s law gives V = IR, where V is voltage in volts, I current in amperes and R resistance in ohms. Power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R.

Example: a 24 V DC heater draws 2.5 A. Its input power is P = 24 × 2.5 = 60 W.

sections.heading: AC and power
sections.text:
Alternating current (AC) reverses periodically. Its frequency is the number of cycles per second (Hz). In a resistive AC circuit, V and I peak and reverse together. With inductive loads such as motors and transformers, current lags voltage by phase angle φ; capacitive loads make it lead. Real power is P = VI cos φ for single phase, using RMS values, where cos φ is the power factor. For a balanced three-phase load, P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ, where V_L and I_L are line voltage and line current.

Example: a 400 V three-phase motor draws 10 A at power factor 0.85. P = √3 × 400 × 10 × 0.85 = 5,889 W, about 5.9 kW.

sections.heading: Transformers and motors
sections.text: A transformer changes AC voltage by mutual induction. Ideal turns ratio: V2/V1 = N2/N1. It does not work on steady DC. An electric motor converts electrical energy to rotation. DC motors are simple to control; AC induction motors are common in industry because they are robust. A variable frequency drive (VFD) changes the frequency and voltage supplied to an AC motor, so its speed can be adjusted.

sections.heading: Sensors and control
sections.text: A sensor converts a physical quantity, such as position, temperature or pressure, into an electrical signal. A switch makes or breaks a circuit; a relay or contactor uses a small current to switch a larger one. Basic control circuits use contacts, pushbuttons and sensors in series or parallel to start, stop or interlock a machine. In automation, drives and sensors feed a controller, often a programmable logic controller (PLC), which decides outputs. Wiring rules and component standards differ by country; work must follow local regulations and be done by qualified people.

keyPoints: Ohm’s law is V = IR; DC power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
Single-phase AC real power is P = VI cos φ; balanced three-phase power is P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ.
An ideal transformer follows V2/V1 = N2/N1 and needs changing AC, not steady DC.
A variable frequency drive controls AC motor speed by changing supply frequency and voltage.
Sensors convert physical quantities into electrical signals; relays and contactors switch larger currents.
Control circuits combine switches and sensors to start, stop and interlock machines; local wiring rules differ by country.

en.title: Metal casting processes
en.short: Sand, shell, investment, die and continuous casting, mould design, solidification and defects.

sections.heading: Sand casting and moulds
sections.text:
Sand casting pours molten metal into a sand mould. A pattern is a replica of the part, made slightly larger to allow for solidification shrinkage. A core forms internal cavities. The gating system (sprue, runner and gates) delivers metal smoothly, and the riser is a reservoir of liquid metal that feeds the casting as it shrinks.

Shell moulding uses a resin-bonded sand shell for better finish and accuracy than green sand, which is clay-bonded sand with moisture.

sections.heading: Other casting processes
sections.text: Investment casting coats a wax pattern with ceramic, melts out the wax and pours metal, giving fine detail. Die casting forces molten metal into a metal die under pressure; it suits high production of non-ferrous parts. Continuous casting solidifies a continuous strand, commonly steel slabs and billets.

sections.heading: Solidification and defects
sections.text:
Solidification starts at the mould wall. Chvorinov’s rule gives solidification time t = k(V/A)², where V is volume, A is cooling surface area and k is a mould constant.

Example: a 100 mm cube has V = 1,000,000 mm³ and A = 60,000 mm², so V/A = 16.7 mm. With k = 0.02 min/mm², t = 0.02 × 16.7² = 5.6 min.

Defects include shrinkage cavities when the riser is too small, gas porosity, misruns from cold metal and hot tears from restrained contraction.

sections.heading: Selecting a process
sections.text:
Choose a process by quantity, metal, size, tolerance, surface finish and cost. Sand casting is flexible and cheap for small batches; die casting is economic at high volume; investment casting gives precision.

Foundry standards and safety rules differ by country: for example, COREN registers engineers in Nigeria. Check current national standards and regulations; do not assume one country’s limits apply elsewhere.

keyPoints: Sand casting uses a sand mould with a pattern, core, gating system and riser.
Shell moulding and investment casting give better surface finish and detail than green sand casting.
Die casting is for high-volume non-ferrous parts, while continuous casting produces long strands such as steel slabs.
Chvorinov’s rule estimates solidification time as t = k(V/A)².
Common defects are shrinkage cavities, gas porosity, misruns and hot tears.
Select a casting process by quantity, metal, tolerance, finish and cost, and check the standards and registration rules of the country concerned.

en.title: Bulk deformation processes: rolling, forging, extrusion and drawing
en.short: Rolling, forging, extrusion and drawing, with flow stress, friction, defects and product properties.

sections.heading: Rolling
sections.text:
Rolling passes metal between rotating rolls to reduce thickness. Hot rolling is above the recrystallisation temperature: flow stress is low, large reductions are possible, and grains refine, but surface scale and tolerances are poorer. Cold rolling is below it: strain hardening raises strength and hardness, surface finish and tolerance improve, and annealing may be needed.

The draft is Δh = h0 − hf and true strain is ε = ln(h0/hf).

sections.heading: Forging and extrusion
sections.text: Forging shapes metal by compressive force, using open dies or closed dies; it is usually hot and can improve toughness by aligning flow lines. Extrusion pushes a billet through a die to make a long profile; in direct extrusion the billet rubs against the container wall, and indirect extrusion avoids this friction. Drawing pulls wire or bar through a die, usually cold, giving accurate size and strength.

sections.heading: Flow stress
sections.text:
Flow stress is the stress needed for continuing plastic flow at a given strain, strain rate and temperature. For cold working, σ = K ε^n, where K is the strength coefficient and n the strain-hardening exponent.

Example: cold rolling reduces thickness from 10 mm to 6 mm, so ε = ln(10/6) = 0.511. With K = 600 MPa and n = 0.2, σ = 600 × 0.511^0.2 ≈ 525 MPa.

sections.heading: Friction and defects
sections.text:
Friction raises force and power, wears dies and makes deformation uneven; lubrication lowers it. Hot working may use glass or graphite, cold drawing soaps or oils. Defects include rolling waviness and edge cracks, forging laps and cold shuts, extrusion piping and die lines, and drawing central bursts.

Temperature, reduction, die angle and friction control grain size, residual stress, strength and ductility. Standards vary by country; check the current national standard.

keyPoints: Hot rolling is above recrystallisation temperature and lowers flow stress; cold rolling strain hardens and improves finish and tolerance.
Forging uses compressive force, extrusion pushes through a die, and drawing pulls through a die.
Flow stress for cold working follows σ = K ε^n, with true strain ε = ln(h0/hf) in rolling.
Friction raises forming force and causes uneven flow; lubrication and die design reduce it.
Common defects include laps, cold shuts, piping, die lines, edge cracks and central bursts.
Process temperature, reduction, die angle and friction affect strength, ductility, grain size and residual stress; standards vary by country.

en.title: Sheet metal forming: shearing, bending and drawing
en.short: Shearing, blanking, bending, deep drawing, stretch forming, springback, formability and press tooling.

sections.heading: Shearing and blanking
sections.text: Shearing cuts sheet between punch and die. Blanking cuts a closed outline so the piece is the product; piercing cuts a hole and the piece is scrap. Clearance affects edges and tool wear. Cutting force is F = τ × L × t, where τ is shear strength, L cut length and t thickness. Example: L = 200 mm, t = 2 mm, τ = 300 N/mm² gives F = 300 × 200 × 2 = 120 kN. Press capacity must exceed this.

sections.heading: Bending and springback
sections.text: Bending forms sheet about a punch radius. Outer fibres stretch, inner fibres compress, and the neutral axis stays unstretched. Bend allowance estimates blank length: L_b = θ(R + Kt), where θ is in radians, R inside radius, t thickness and K the neutral-axis factor. Springback is elastic recovery after the punch leaves: the bend angle opens and the radius grows. It is greater with high yield strength, large R/t and thin sheet. Overbending, bottoming or coining reduce it.

sections.heading: Drawing and formability
sections.text: Deep drawing pushes a blank into a die; the flange shrinks and the wall stretches. Draw ratio DR = blank diameter ÷ punch diameter. Excessive DR tears; redrawing helps. Stretch forming clamps the sheet and pulls it over a form block, with no flange. Formability is safe deformation before necking or fracture. A forming limit diagram (FLD) plots major against minor strain; its curve separates safe from failed strains. Defects include wrinkling, tearing, earing (uneven ears on the cup rim) and orange peel (rough, pebbled surface). Limits vary with material, thickness and lubrication.

sections.heading: Press tooling and dies
sections.text: Presses are crank or hydraulic. A die set holds punch and die in alignment. Blanking dies cut outlines; bending dies form angles; drawing dies control flow with a blank holder and draw beads. Design principles include clearance, suitable punch and die radii, blank-holder force, lubrication, guidance, scrap removal and guarding. Tool steel and surface treatment affect wear. Codes, standards and registration differ by country, such as COREN in Nigeria; check the local standard.

keyPoints: Shearing cuts sheet between punch and die; blanking makes the cut piece the product, while piercing makes it scrap.
Cutting force estimate: F = τ × L × t, with τ shear strength, L cut length and t thickness.
Bend allowance: L_b = θ(R + Kt), with θ in radians; K depends on material and tooling.
Springback is elastic recovery that opens the bend and increases the radius; overbending or coining can reduce it.
Deep drawing draw ratio: DR = blank diameter ÷ punch diameter; excessive DR causes tearing, and redrawing helps.
Forming limit diagrams plot major against minor strain and separate safe from failed forming; die design controls clearance, radii, blank-holder force and lubrication.

en.title: Machining and cutting tools
en.short: Turning, milling and drilling; tool geometry and materials; chips, forces, wear, Taylor tool life and fluids.

sections.heading: Turning, milling, drilling
sections.text:
Machining removes metal as chips with a harder tool. In turning the workpiece rotates and a single-point tool feeds along it. In milling a multi-tooth cutter rotates while the work feeds past. In drilling a rotating drill makes a hole. Boring enlarges a hole, reaming finishes it, tapping cuts a thread.

Cutting speed is the surface speed in m/min; feed is the movement per revolution or per tooth; depth of cut is the thickness removed in one pass.

sections.heading: Tool geometry and materials
sections.text:
A single-point tool has a rake angle, a clearance angle, a cutting-edge angle and a nose radius. Positive rake lowers cutting force but weakens the edge; negative rake strengthens it for hard work.

Tool materials must stay hard when hot: high-speed steel, cemented carbide, coated carbide, ceramics, cubic boron nitride and diamond, roughly in order of hot hardness and brittleness.

sections.heading: Chips, forces, wear, life
sections.text:
Continuous chips give a good finish; discontinuous chips form in brittle metals; a built-up edge is work metal welded to the edge that then breaks away. Cutting force Fc and thrust force Ft are measured with a dynamometer.

Heat arises in the shear zone and at the rake face, and most leaves with the chip, so fluid cooling is limited. Wear shows as flank wear and crater wear. Taylor’s equation: VT^n = C.

Example: n = 0.25, C = 200. At V = 100 m/min, T = (200/100)^4 = 16 min.

sections.heading: Machinability and fluids
sections.text:
Machinability means how easily a material cuts: long tool life, low force, good finish. Sulphur and lead additions improve it in steel, but lead is toxic.

Cutting fluids remove heat and lubricate. Water-based soluble oils cool best at high speed; neat oils lubricate best at low speed. Choice depends on material, operation and health rules, which vary by country.

keyPoints: Turning rotates the work; milling rotates a multi-tooth cutter; drilling rotates the drill.
Positive rake reduces cutting force but weakens the edge.
Tool materials rank by hot hardness: HSS, carbide, ceramic, CBN, diamond.
Taylor tool life: VT^n = C, with n and C found by cutting tests.
Most cutting heat leaves with the chip, not the tool.
Water-based fluids cool; neat oils lubricate.

en.title: Abrasive, non-traditional and finishing processes
en.short: Grinding, honing, lapping, EDM, laser and waterjet cutting, plus surface finishing and coatings.

sections.heading: Abrasive processes
sections.text:
Abrasive processes remove material with hard particles. Grinding uses a rotating bonded wheel whose edges cut small chips; it suits hard materials, close tolerances and fine finishes. Honing uses bonded stones pressed against a bore while rotating and reciprocating, producing a cross-hatch pattern and correcting roundness. Lapping uses loose abrasive slurry between the lap and workpiece to improve flatness and finish. Superfinishing uses a low-pressure oscillating stone to remove a thin damaged layer.

Wheel speed is v = πDN. For D = 250 mm = 0.25 m and N = 1800 rev/min = 30 rev/s: v = π × 0.25 × 30 = 23.6 m/s. Check wheel rating and machine limits before running.

sections.heading: Non-traditional cutting
sections.text:
Non-traditional processes remove material without a conventional cutting tool. Electrical discharge machining (EDM) uses repeated sparks between a shaped electrode and a conductive workpiece in an insulating dielectric fluid. The sparks melt and vaporise tiny amounts of metal, so EDM can cut hardened steel and complex dies with little cutting force. Laser cutting focuses a beam to melt or vaporise a narrow path, giving a small heat-affected zone. Waterjet cutting uses a high-pressure water jet, often with abrasive particles, to cut metals, stone and composites without a heat-affected zone.

Choice depends on material, thickness, tolerance, edge quality and cost. Safety rules vary by country, so check the current local standard and the machine maker’s data.

sections.heading: Finishing and coatings
sections.text: Finishing changes the surface without necessarily changing bulk shape. Cleaning and deburring remove dirt and sharp edges. Polishing and buffing use fine abrasives to reduce roughness. Shot blasting cleans or prepares a surface, and shot peening induces compressive stress to resist fatigue. Coatings include electroplating, anodising of aluminium, conversion coatings, painting, powder coating, and physical vapour deposition (PVD) and chemical vapour deposition (CVD). Coating choice depends on adhesion, corrosion and wear resistance, appearance, cost and environmental rules, which differ by country. Test coupons and the supplier’s data sheet should guide the process.

keyPoints: Grinding uses a rotating bonded abrasive wheel; wheel speed is v = πDN.
Honing corrects bore shape, lapping uses loose slurry for flatness, and superfinishing removes a thin damaged layer.
EDM removes conductive metal by sparks in an insulating fluid, with little cutting force.
Laser and waterjet cut without a solid tool; waterjet leaves no heat-affected zone.
Finishing includes polishing, blasting, peening, plating, anodising and vapour deposition.
Process and coating choices depend on material, tolerance, cost and local safety and environmental rules.

en.title: Joining and assembly processes
en.short: Arc, resistance, gas and solid-state welding, brazing, soldering, adhesives, fasteners and assembly.

sections.heading: Welding methods
sections.text: Welding joins metals by melting or pressure. Arc welding uses an electric arc between an electrode and the work to melt base metal and filler; common versions are shielded metal arc, metal inert gas (MIG) and tungsten inert gas (TIG). Resistance welding passes a large current through the joint; contact resistance heats it and pressure forges it, as in spot welding. Gas welding uses a fuel-gas flame, usually oxy-acetylene, to melt the edges. Solid-state welding joins without bulk melting, using pressure, friction or diffusion; friction welding is an example.

sections.heading: Brazing and bonding
sections.text: Brazing and soldering melt a filler but not the base metal. Brazing uses a filler that melts above about 450 °C; soldering uses one that melts below that, commonly for electronics. Adhesive bonding uses a polymer adhesive; it spreads load over an area and suits dissimilar materials, but needs clean surfaces and cure time. Mechanical fastening uses bolts, screws, rivets or clips. Bolts and screws allow dismantling; rivets are permanent. Fasteners add weight and can loosen under vibration.

sections.heading: Joints and inspection
sections.text: Joint design chooses lap, butt, T or corner joints and sets gap, edge preparation and access. Poor design concentrates stress and traps slag. Welding heat creates a heat-affected zone (HAZ), where microstructure and hardness change; it also causes distortion and residual stress. Defects include porosity, slag, incomplete fusion, undercut and cracks. Inspection starts with visual checks, then may use dye penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic or radiographic testing. Acceptance limits and inspector rules differ by country and product, so check the current national or international code.

sections.heading: Assembly methods
sections.text: Assembly may be manual, fixed-position, flow-line or automated. Design for assembly reduces part count and makes parts easy to align and fasten. Case: a small workshop making steel chairs can arc-weld the frame for strength and low cost, then bolt the seat so it can be replaced. An aluminium electronics case may be better riveted or adhesively bonded, because welding heat could distort it.

keyPoints: Arc welding melts with an electric arc; resistance welding uses current and pressure; gas welding uses a flame; solid-state welding avoids bulk melting.
Brazing and soldering melt filler only, with brazing above about 450 °C and soldering below.
Adhesive bonding spreads load and suits dissimilar materials; bolts and screws allow dismantling but can loosen.
Welding heat creates a heat-affected zone, distortion and residual stress, so joint design and heat control matter.
Common weld defects include porosity, slag, incomplete fusion, undercut and cracks; inspection ranges from visual checks to radiographic testing.
Assembly can be manual, flow-line or automated; design for assembly reduces part count and eases alignment.

en.title: Polymer processing, composites and additive manufacturing
en.short: Injection moulding, extrusion, blow moulding, composite lay-up and 3D printing processes and materials.

sections.heading: Polymer processing
sections.text:
Most polymer products start as thermoplastic granules or thermoset resin. In injection moulding, a screw melts the polymer and forces it into a closed mould; the part cools and is ejected. It suits complex, high-volume parts, but moulds are costly. Extrusion is continuous: the screw pushes melt through a die to make pipe, film or profiles. Blow moulding forms hollow articles: a heated tube (parison) is inflated against a mould cavity, as for bottles.

Example: clamp force must exceed projected area × cavity pressure. For area 0.008 m² and pressure 40 MPa: 0.008 × 40,000,000 = 320,000 N = 320 kN. A safety margin is added; values vary with material and part.

sections.heading: Composite lay-up
sections.text: Composites combine strong fibres, such as glass or carbon, with a matrix resin that holds them and shares load. Lay-up places fibre plies in chosen directions. Hand lay-up and spray-up are simple but labour-intensive. Vacuum bagging compacts the laminate and removes air; autoclave curing gives higher fibre fraction and lower void content. Resin transfer moulding injects resin into a closed fibre preform. Properties are directional, so ply orientation matters. Curing and quality control follow the material system and application; standards differ by country.

sections.heading: Additive manufacturing
sections.text: Additive manufacturing (3D printing) builds a part layer by layer from a CAD model. Material extrusion (often FDM) melts thermoplastic filament through a nozzle. Vat photopolymerisation cures liquid resin with light. Powder bed fusion spreads polymer or metal powder and fuses selected areas with a laser or electron beam. Binder jetting prints a binder into powder. Materials include thermoplastics, photopolymers, metals and ceramics. AM suits prototypes, customised parts, small batches and complex internal channels, but it is often slower and more costly per part than moulding at high volume. Properties can be anisotropic; post-processing and qualification depend on the application and country.

keyPoints: Injection moulding melts polymer and injects it into a closed mould; it suits high volume but needs costly tooling.
Extrusion is continuous through a die; blow moulding inflates a parison to make hollow parts.
Clamp force must exceed projected area × cavity pressure; 0.008 m² at 40 MPa needs 320 kN.
Composite lay-up places oriented fibres in a resin matrix; vacuum bagging and autoclave curing reduce voids.
Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer; common methods are material extrusion, vat photopolymerisation and powder bed fusion.
AM suits prototypes, custom parts and complex geometry, but properties can be anisotropic and qualification varies by application and country.

en.title: Metrology, tolerances and surface finish
en.short: Instruments and calibration, limits and fits, tolerance stacks, GD&T, surface texture and inspection.

sections.heading: Measurement and calibration
sections.text: Metrology is the science of measurement. Instruments include the vernier caliper, micrometer, dial indicator, height gauge and coordinate measuring machine (CMM). Calibration compares an instrument with a traceable reference linked to the International System of Units (SI). The calibration record gives deviation and measurement uncertainty, the interval within which the true value is expected to lie. Uncalibrated instruments cannot support interchangeability or quality claims.

sections.heading: Limits and fits
sections.text:
A limit is an allowed maximum or minimum size; tolerance is the difference between them. ISO 286, an international standard, uses tolerance grades and letters for holes (capital) and shafts (lowercase) to define clearance, transition and interference fits. National standards may differ.

Example, not a code value: hole 25.000 to 25.021 mm, shaft 24.980 to 24.993 mm.
Maximum clearance = 25.021 − 24.980 = 0.041 mm.
Minimum clearance = 25.000 − 24.993 = 0.007 mm.
Both positive, so this is a clearance fit. Hole tolerance = 0.021 mm; shaft tolerance = 0.013 mm.

sections.heading: Tolerances and GD&T
sections.text:
Tolerance analysis predicts how variations combine. Worst-case analysis adds tolerances: T = ΣTi. Statistical root-sum-square (RSS) assumes independent random errors: T = √(ΣTi²). For 0.10, 0.15 and 0.20 mm, worst case = 0.45 mm; RSS = √(0.10² + 0.15² + 0.20²) = √0.0725 = 0.269 mm.

Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T) controls form, orientation, location, profile and runout using a feature control frame and datums. ISO 1101 is international; ASME Y14.5 is used in the United States. Check the edition and national adoption.

sections.heading: Surface and inspection
sections.text:
Surface texture has roughness (short wavelengths), waviness and lay, the direction of the dominant surface pattern. Ra is the arithmetic mean deviation of the roughness profile; Rz is a peak-to-valley height whose exact definition depends on the standard. A stylus profilometer or optical instrument measures it.

Inspection checks conformance. A go/no-go gauge gives a fast pass or fail: the go gauge should pass, the no-go should not. Measurement gives a value and uncertainty. Interchangeability depends on specified tolerances, capable processes and traceable measurement.

keyPoints: Calibration compares an instrument with a traceable reference and records measurement uncertainty.
For a hole and shaft, clearance = hole size − shaft size; tolerance = upper limit − lower limit.
Worst-case tolerance stack-up is T = ΣTi; independent random tolerances combine as T = √(ΣTi²).
GD&T controls form, orientation, location, profile and runout relative to datums.
Surface texture includes roughness, waviness and lay; Ra is a common roughness parameter.
Go/no-go gauges give fast pass/fail inspection, while measurement gives a value and uncertainty.

en.title: Production planning and control
en.short: Forecasting, aggregate planning, MPS, MRP, capacity, inventory and shop-floor scheduling.

sections.heading: Forecasting and aggregate planning
sections.text:
Forecasting estimates future demand from past data and judgement. Simple methods include moving averages and exponential smoothing. Forecast error is measured and used to revise the forecast.

Aggregate planning matches total supply to expected demand over a medium horizon, often several months. It sets overall production rate, workforce size and inventory levels. It does not schedule individual products.

sections.heading: Master scheduling and MRP
sections.text:
The master production schedule (MPS) breaks the aggregate plan into end products by time period. Material requirements planning (MRP) uses the MPS, the bill of materials (BOM), inventory records and lead times to calculate component needs and planned orders.

Net requirement = gross requirement + safety stock − on hand − scheduled receipts.

Example: one end product needs two components. The MPS calls for 100 products. Component stock is 30, a scheduled receipt is 20, and safety stock is 10.
Gross requirement = 100 × 2 = 200
Net requirement = 200 + 10 − 30 − 20 = 160 components.

sections.heading: Capacity and inventory
sections.text:
Capacity planning compares load, the work required in machine or labour hours, with available capacity. Rough-cut capacity planning checks the MPS; capacity requirements planning checks MRP. If load exceeds capacity, the plan must change.

Inventory control sets order size and timing. The economic order quantity (EOQ) balances ordering cost and holding cost:
EOQ = √(2DS ÷ H)
where D is annual demand, S order cost, H holding cost per unit per year.

Example: D = 10,000 units, S = 200, H = 4.
EOQ = √(2 × 10,000 × 200 ÷ 4) = √(1,000,000) = 1,000 units.

sections.heading: Shop-floor scheduling
sections.text:
Shop-floor scheduling turns planned orders into sequences on machines. Forward scheduling starts from release date; backward scheduling starts from due date. Priority rules such as earliest due date or shortest processing time choose the next job.

Planning, capacity and operations must agree. A schedule is feasible only when materials, capacity and lead times are available. Actual output feeds back into forecasts, inventory records and future plans.

keyPoints: Forecasting estimates demand; aggregate planning sets total output, workforce and inventory over a medium horizon.
The MPS disaggregates the aggregate plan into end products by time period.
MRP net requirement = gross requirement + safety stock − on hand − scheduled receipts.
Capacity planning compares load with available capacity; an infeasible plan must be revised.
EOQ = √(2DS ÷ H) sets order size, and reorder point = demand during lead time + safety stock sets timing.
Shop-floor scheduling sequences jobs; feedback keeps plans feasible and current.

en.title: Work study, method study and ergonomics
en.short: Method study, process charts, time study, standard time, productivity and ergonomic job design.

sections.heading: Method study
sections.text: Method study is the systematic recording and critical examination of how a job is done, to remove unnecessary work and design a better method. The usual sequence is select, record, examine, develop, install and maintain. Process charts record the sequence of events with symbols for operation, inspection, transport, delay and storage. A flow process chart follows the material or the worker; a two-handed chart records both hands. The aim is to question each step: why, what, where, when, who and how.

sections.heading: Work measurement
sections.text: Work measurement sets the time a trained worker needs at a defined performance. Time study divides the job into elements, times each with a stopwatch, rates the pace and adds allowances for rest, personal needs and delays. Standard time = observed time × rating factor × (1 + allowance). Example: observed time 8.0 min, rating 110% (1.10), allowance 15% (0.15). Basic time = 8.0 × 1.10 = 8.8 min. Standard time = 8.8 × 1.15 = 10.12 min. Allowance rates and rating methods vary by organisation and country.

sections.heading: Productivity
sections.text: Productivity compares output with input. Labour productivity can be standard hours produced ÷ hours paid. If 120 standard hours are produced in 150 paid hours, productivity = 120 ÷ 150 = 0.80, or 80%. Higher productivity means less waste, not necessarily harder work.

sections.heading: Ergonomics and job design
sections.text: Ergonomics, or human factors, fits the work, equipment and workplace to human abilities and limits. Anthropometry gives body dimensions for reach, clearance and seat height. Good design reduces fatigue and errors by considering posture, force, repetition, lighting, noise and controls. Job design may use rotation, enlargement or enrichment. Legal exposure limits and manual handling rules differ by country; check the current national safety law.

keyPoints: Method study follows select, record, examine, develop, install and maintain.
Process charts use symbols for operation, inspection, transport, delay and storage.
Standard time = observed time × rating factor × (1 + allowance).
An observed time of 8.0 min at 110% rating with 15% allowance gives a standard time of 10.12 min.
Labour productivity = standard hours produced ÷ hours paid.
Ergonomics fits work to people; legal exposure and manual handling limits vary by country.

en.title: Quality management and statistical process control
en.short: Quality costs, ISO 9001, control charts, capability, acceptance sampling and Six Sigma.

sections.heading: Quality and costs
sections.text: Quality means meeting agreed requirements and giving customer satisfaction, not necessarily the highest grade. Quality costs are grouped as prevention (training, design review), appraisal (inspection, testing), internal failure (scrap, rework) and external failure (warranty, recalls). Failure costs usually fall as prevention rises, but the total has a minimum; the exact balance varies by firm.

sections.heading: Assurance and ISO 9001
sections.text: Quality control checks the product; quality assurance builds the system that makes defects less likely. A quality management system (QMS) sets documented processes, responsibilities and improvement. ISO 9001 is an international standard for QMS, based on customer focus, process approach and risk-based thinking; certification is by accredited bodies. National rules and professional registration differ, so check the relevant country’s requirements.

sections.heading: Control charts and capability
sections.text:
Statistical process control plots a measured characteristic over time. On an x-bar chart for sample means, control limits are μ ± 3σ/√n, where σ is the process standard deviation and n the sample size. Points outside the limits, or trends, show special-cause (assignable) variation. Example: μ = 50, σ = 2, n = 4 gives limits 50 ± 3(2/√4) = 47 and 53.

Process capability compares specification width with process spread: Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ (6σ) and Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) ÷ (3σ). For USL 10.2, LSL 9.8, μ 10.0, σ 0.05: Cp = 0.4 ÷ 0.3 = 1.33, and Cpk = 0.2 ÷ 0.15 = 1.33.

sections.heading: Sampling and Six Sigma
sections.text: Acceptance sampling decides whether to accept a lot from a sample. AQL is the worst quality level that is still acceptable as a process average; LTPD is a poor level a consumer wants rejected. Producer’s risk α is rejecting a good lot; consumer’s risk β is accepting a bad lot. Six Sigma is an improvement method using DMAIC (define, measure, analyse, improve, control). The six-sigma level is often quoted as 3.4 defects per million opportunities, assuming a 1.5σ shift; check the definition used.

keyPoints: Quality costs are prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure.
ISO 9001 is an international QMS standard; certification and national requirements vary.
Control limits for sample means are μ ± 3σ/√n.
Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ (6σ); Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) ÷ (3σ).
Acceptance sampling balances producer’s risk α and consumer’s risk β using AQL and LTPD.
Six Sigma uses DMAIC and aims at very low defect rates; the 3.4 DPMO figure assumes a 1.5σ shift.

en.title: Lean manufacturing and just-in-time
en.short: Lean principles, value stream mapping, waste, JIT, kanban, set-up reduction and cells.

sections.heading: Lean thinking
sections.text: Lean manufacturing organises production to deliver customer value with least waste. Value is what the customer pays for; waste (muda) is any activity that consumes resources without adding value. Principles: specify value, map the value stream, create flow, let the customer pull, pursue perfection. Value stream mapping charts steps from order to delivery and separates value-adding from non-value-adding time.

sections.heading: The wastes
sections.text: The seven wastes are transport, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, overprocessing and defects. Overproduction is often the worst because it hides problems and ties up cash. Waste elimination removes causes, not symptoms. Case: a workshop keeps a week of chair frames between cutting and assembly. Mapping shows about a week of waiting. Smaller batches and closer assembly cut waiting and floor space.

sections.heading: JIT and kanban
sections.text: Just-in-time (JIT) means producing what the next step needs, when needed, in the quantity needed. It is a pull system: a downstream operation signals demand upstream. A kanban is a card or signal authorising production or withdrawal of a standard container. Takt time sets the pace: takt time = available working time ÷ customer demand. Example: 450 minutes available, demand 480 units: 450 ÷ 480 = 0.9375 min, or 56.25 s per unit. Kanban count (common form): N = D × L × (1 + s) ÷ C. With D = 480/day, L = 0.5 day, s = 0.10, C = 20: N = 480 × 0.5 × 1.10 ÷ 20 = 13.2, so 14 cards.

sections.heading: Set-up, cells, limits
sections.text: Set-up reduction (SMED, single-minute exchange of die) separates internal set-up, machine stopped, from external set-up, machine running, and converts internal work to external. Cellular manufacturing groups machines into a cell making a family of similar parts, enabling one-piece flow. Continuous improvement (kaizen) is ongoing small-step improvement by the people doing the work. Lean suits stable, repetitive demand and reliable suppliers. It is weaker with high variety, volatile demand or long, unreliable supply lines, where buffers may be needed. It also depends on respect for people, not only tools.

keyPoints: Lean delivers customer value with least waste by specifying value, mapping the stream, creating flow, pulling and improving.
The seven wastes are transport, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, overprocessing and defects.
JIT is a pull system; kanban signals authorise production or withdrawal.
Takt time = available working time ÷ customer demand.
Kanban count N = D × L × (1 + s) ÷ C, rounded up.
SMED, cells and kaizen support flow, but lean needs stable demand and reliable supply; buffers may be needed otherwise.

en.title: Automation, robotics and CNC machines
en.short: Automation levels, sensors, PLCs, industrial robots, CNC machines, workholding and integration.

sections.heading: Automation levels
sections.text: Automation uses control systems to replace or assist human work in a process. Fixed automation uses dedicated equipment for one high-volume task. Programmable automation can be reprogrammed for batches. Flexible automation can change between products with little changeover. The automation hierarchy runs from sensors and actuators at the machine, through programmable logic controllers and cells, to plant supervision. Separating levels keeps fast machine control apart from slower planning.

sections.heading: Sensors and PLCs
sections.text: Sensors measure physical variables such as position, proximity, pressure, temperature, force and flow, and convert them into signals. Actuators convert control signals into motion; common types are electric motors, pneumatic cylinders and hydraulic cylinders. A programmable logic controller (PLC) is an industrial computer with input and output modules. It repeats a scan cycle: read the inputs, execute the stored program, then update the outputs. Ladder logic is a common programming form.

sections.heading: Robots and CNC
sections.text: An industrial robot has a manipulator with joints, a controller and an end effector. Its axes give degrees of freedom; payload, reach, accuracy and repeatability describe its capability. Accuracy is closeness to the commanded point; repeatability is closeness of repeated visits. A CNC machine reads a part program of G-codes and M-codes and moves axes under feedback control. G-codes control motion; M-codes control machine functions such as spindle and coolant. For milling, feed rate is f = fz × z × N, where fz is feed per tooth, z is the number of teeth and N is spindle speed. Example: fz = 0.1 mm/tooth, z = 4, N = 1200 rpm, so f = 0.1 × 4 × 1200 = 480 mm/min.

sections.heading: Workholding and integration
sections.text: Workholding locates the part and clamps it against cutting forces. A good fixture gives repeatable position, supports the part, and leaves tool access. Integration links machines with robots, pallets, conveyors and sensors. Robot tending, automatic tool changes and interlocks allow unattended running. Safety rules for automated cells vary by country, so check the current local regulations.

keyPoints: Fixed automation suits high volume; programmable and flexible automation suit batches and product changes.
A PLC repeats a scan cycle: read inputs, execute the program, update outputs.
Sensors convert physical variables into signals; actuators convert control signals into motion.
Industrial robots are described by degrees of freedom, payload, reach, accuracy and repeatability.
For milling, CNC feed rate is f = fz × z × N; with fz = 0.1 mm/tooth, z = 4 and N = 1200 rpm, f = 480 mm/min.
Workholding must locate and clamp the part rigidly without blocking tool access or over-constraining it.

en.title: CAD/CAM and computer-integrated manufacturing
en.short: CAD data, process planning, CAM and NC programming, data exchange and factory information systems.

sections.heading: CAD data
sections.text: Computer-aided design (CAD) creates a product model in a computer. The model may be wireframe, surface or solid. A solid model represents a closed volume, so it can supply mass properties and support downstream work. Feature-based and parametric CAD stores dimensions and relationships, so changing a parameter rebuilds the geometry. The CAD database holds geometry, assembly structure, materials and metadata. Good data management controls versions and access.

sections.heading: CAPP and CAM
sections.text: Computer-aided process planning (CAPP) decides the operations, machines, tools and sequence needed to make a part. Variant CAPP retrieves a similar old plan and edits it. Generative CAPP builds a plan from rules and part features, but it needs reliable manufacturing knowledge. Computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) takes CAD geometry and generates tool paths, simulates cutting and checks collisions. A post-processor converts the tool path into code for a particular machine controller.

sections.heading: NC part programming
sections.text: NC part programming writes the instructions for numerical control (NC) machine tools. Manual programming uses G-codes and coordinates; CAM generates most programs today. A program defines the workpiece zero, tool changes, feeds, speeds and motion. Example: a linear cut from (0, 0) to (50, 20) mm at feed 200 mm/min. Path length = √(50² + 20²) = √2900 = 53.85 mm. Time = 53.85 ÷ 200 = 0.269 min, about 16.2 s.

sections.heading: CIM and data exchange
sections.text: Computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM) links design, planning, production and business information through shared computer systems. Data exchange lets different CAD/CAM systems share models. Neutral formats include IGES and STEP; DXF is common for drawings. Features and history may be lost, so check the exported model. The factory information system collects orders, stock, machine status and quality data and shares it with planning and control. CIM is an integration strategy, not a single product.

keyPoints: CAD stores geometry and product data; solid and feature-based models support downstream use.
CAPP plans operations and sequence; variant CAPP reuses old plans, generative CAPP derives new ones.
CAM converts CAD geometry into tool paths and post-processes them into NC code.
NC programs use coordinates, feeds and speeds; for a straight cut, length = √(Δx² + Δy²) and time = length ÷ feed.
IGES and STEP are neutral formats for exchanging CAD data between systems.
CIM integrates design, planning, manufacturing and business data; the factory information system supplies the shared data.

en.title: Maintenance and reliability engineering
en.short: Maintenance strategies, reliability measures, FMEA, spares planning, TPM and OEE.

sections.heading: Maintenance strategies
sections.text: Breakdown maintenance runs equipment until it fails. It suits cheap, non-critical items but risks secondary damage and long stops. Preventive maintenance replaces or services items on a fixed schedule, whether or not they are degrading. Predictive maintenance uses condition data to forecast failure, while condition-based maintenance acts when a measured value passes a limit. Condition monitoring includes vibration, oil analysis, thermography and ultrasound. Predictive and condition-based overlap in practice; both aim to intervene only when needed.

sections.heading: Reliability measures
sections.text: Reliability R(t) is the probability that an item performs its required function for a stated time under stated conditions. For a constant failure rate λ, R(t) = e^(−λt) and MTBF = 1 ÷ λ, where MTBF is mean time between failures for a repairable item. Availability A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR), where MTTR is mean time to repair. Example: λ = 0.002 per hour, t = 500 h. R = e^(−1) = 0.368. MTBF = 1 ÷ 0.002 = 500 h. With MTTR = 10 h, A = 500 ÷ 510 = 0.980.

sections.heading: FMEA and planning
sections.text: Failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA) lists each failure mode, its effect and cause, then scores severity, occurrence and detection. The risk priority number RPN = severity × occurrence × detection ranks risks; scales vary, so use the organisation’s own. Maintenance planning sets work orders, priorities and schedules. Spare-parts policy weighs holding cost against downtime cost, using criticality, lead time and failure rate.

sections.heading: TPM and OEE
sections.text: Total productive maintenance (TPM) involves operators in autonomous maintenance, planned maintenance and continuous improvement, aiming for zero breakdowns. Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) = availability × performance × quality. Example: planned production time 480 min, downtime 48 min, run time 432 min, ideal cycle 1 min/unit, total 400 units, good 380. Availability = 432 ÷ 480 = 0.900. Performance = (1 × 400) ÷ 432 = 0.926. Quality = 380 ÷ 400 = 0.950. OEE = 0.900 × 0.926 × 0.950 = 0.792, about 79%.

keyPoints: Breakdown maintenance suits cheap non-critical items; preventive is time-based; predictive and condition-based act on measured condition.
For constant failure rate, R(t) = e^(−λt) and MTBF = 1 ÷ λ.
Availability A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR).
FMEA ranks risks by RPN = severity × occurrence × detection, but scales vary.
OEE = availability × performance × quality.
Spare-parts policy balances holding cost against downtime cost using criticality, lead time and failure rate.

en.title: Engineering economy and cost estimation
en.short: Time value of money, depreciation, tax, cost estimation, make-or-buy and replacement decisions.

sections.heading: Time value
sections.text:
Money has a time value because it can earn interest. Future worth F = P(1+i)^n and present worth P = F ÷ (1+i)^n, where i is the rate per period and n the period count. For uniform annual A, P = A[(1+i)^n − 1] ÷ [i(1+i)^n]; annual worth reverses this. Rate of return makes present worth zero. Simple payback = initial cost ÷ annual net inflow; it ignores timing.

Example: a machine costs 1,000,000 and saves 300,000 yearly for five years. At i = 10%, PW of savings = 300,000 × 3.7908 = 1,137,240, so NPW ≈ 137,240. Payback = 1,000,000 ÷ 300,000 = 3.33 years.

sections.heading: Depreciation and tax
sections.text: Depreciation spreads an asset’s cost over its useful life; it is an accounting allocation, not cash. Straight line: D = (cost − salvage) ÷ n. Declining balance applies a fixed rate to book value. Taxable income = revenue − cash expenses − depreciation. Tax = rate × taxable income. Depreciation lowers tax, so after-tax cash flow = (revenue − expenses)(1 − t) + tD, where t is the tax rate. Rules vary by country and year; check the tax authority.

sections.heading: Cost estimation
sections.text: Cost estimation predicts the resources needed for a product or project. Product cost includes material, direct labour, overhead and tooling. Project cost includes capital, operating cost and working capital. Methods range from rough order-of-magnitude to definitive estimates. The cost-capacity equation C2 = C1(Q2 ÷ Q1)^n scales cost with capacity; n is an empirical exponent. Learning curves reduce labour time as output rises. Always state the basis, date and currency.

sections.heading: Decisions
sections.text: Make-or-buy compares avoidable making costs with the purchase price, plus quality, capacity and supplier risk. Ignore allocated fixed costs that do not change. Equipment replacement compares the existing asset (the defender) with the proposed new asset (the challenger) using present worth or annual worth over the same study period. Sunk costs are irrelevant. Choose the option with the lower equivalent cost or higher net present worth.

keyPoints: Future worth F = P(1+i)^n; present worth P = F ÷ (1+i)^n.
Uniform series: P = A[(1+i)^n − 1] ÷ [i(1+i)^n] and A = P[i(1+i)^n] ÷ [(1+i)^n − 1].
Rate of return is the i that makes net present worth zero; simple payback ignores time value.
Straight-line depreciation: D = (cost − salvage) ÷ n; after-tax cash flow = (revenue − expenses)(1 − t) + tD.
Cost-capacity scaling: C2 = C1(Q2 ÷ Q1)^n.
For make-or-buy and replacement, compare relevant after-tax cash flows using present worth or annual worth.

en.title: Industrial safety and environmental management
en.short: Hazard identification, risk assessment, guarding, electrical and fire safety, PPE, waste and ISO 14001/45001.

sections.heading: Hazards and risk
sections.text:
A hazard is a source of harm; risk is the chance and severity of that harm. Identify hazards by inspection, operator discussion, incident records and task review. Production hazards include moving parts, electricity, heat, noise, dust, chemicals and manual handling.

Risk assessment scores likelihood × severity. Example: a press feed scores likelihood 4 and severity 5, so risk = 20. An interlocked guard cuts likelihood to 1, giving risk = 5. Controls follow a hierarchy: eliminate, substitute, engineer, administrate, then personal protective equipment (PPE). PPE is last because it protects only the wearer and can fail.

sections.heading: Guarding and electrical
sections.text: Machine guarding places a barrier or interlock between the operator and a danger point such as a nip point (where moving parts can trap you), blade or press. Guards must prevent access without blocking normal work; interlocks stop the machine when a guard opens. Electrical safety uses isolation and lockout/tagout (locking off supplies and tagging them so they cannot be switched on) before maintenance, insulation in good condition, earthing, residual current devices and competent persons.

sections.heading: Fire and PPE
sections.text: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat. Control hot work, store flammables safely, keep extinguishers and exits clear, and practise evacuation. PPE such as eye protection, gloves, hearing protection and respiratory masks is selected from the risk assessment and must fit and be maintained.

sections.heading: Environment and standards
sections.text:
Production affects the environment through energy and water use, air emissions, noise, waste and hazardous substances. The waste hierarchy is prevent, reuse, recycle, recover energy, then dispose. Pollution control starts at source: change processes, contain spills, treat effluent and emissions, and monitor. Environmental limits and permits vary by country, so check the national regulator.

ISO 14001 is the international standard for environmental management systems; ISO 45001 is for occupational health and safety management systems. Both use a plan-do-check-act cycle and require legal requirements, objectives, operational control, monitoring and improvement. Certification is voluntary and done by accredited bodies. Safety law, codes and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria, for example, COREN registers engineers. Check the current national law and code.

keyPoints: A hazard is a source of harm; risk combines the likelihood and severity of harm.
Risk score = likelihood × severity; controls follow eliminate, substitute, engineer, administrate, then PPE.
Machine guards and interlocks prevent access to danger points; electrical work needs isolation, lockout/tagout and competent persons.
Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat; control hot work and keep extinguishers and exits clear.
The waste hierarchy is prevent, reuse, recycle, recover, then dispose; pollution control starts at source.
ISO 14001 covers environmental management systems and ISO 45001 covers occupational health and safety management systems; safety law and registration differ by country, such as COREN in Nigeria.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and regulation
en.short: Codes, competence, public safety and how engineering is regulated and accredited by country.

sections.heading: Codes and ethics
sections.text: Professional ethics are the standards a practitioner uses when duties to employers, clients, colleagues and the public conflict. A code of conduct turns these standards into rules: work within your competence, be honest about results, keep confidences, declare conflicts of interest, and put public safety and the environment before profit. Codes differ in detail between institutions and countries, so read the code that governs you.

sections.heading: Competence and safety
sections.text: Competence means having the knowledge, skill and judgement to do a task safely. A production engineer may sign off a fixture, a pressure system or a process change, so an unverified assumption can injure operators. Competent practice includes checking calculations, using approved standards, recording decisions and asking for specialist help. If a design is unsafe, the duty to warn and stop work can outweigh loyalty to an employer. Negligence is failure to take the care a competent engineer would take.

sections.heading: Institutions and registration
sections.text: Engineering institutions and regulators have separate roles. Learned societies, such as the Nigerian Society of Engineers, support members and set professional expectations. Regulators may license practice and protect titles. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering. In the United Kingdom, the Engineering Council maintains the national register and works with licensed professional bodies. In the United States, ABET accredits university programmes, while state boards license engineers. Requirements, titles and renewal rules differ, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Case and check
sections.text: Case: a junior engineer at a Lagos fabrication firm finds a lifting bracket made from the wrong grade of steel. She records the finding, tells her supervisor and refuses to certify the bracket. The firm replaces it and reviews its material checks. The lesson is not that rules guarantee safety; it is that documented, competent dissent gives safety a chance.

keyPoints: A professional code sets duties such as competence, honesty, confidentiality and public safety.
Work only within your competence and seek specialist help when a task exceeds it.
Public safety can override loyalty to an employer; record and escalate concerns.
Registration and protected titles differ by country; COREN regulates engineering in Nigeria, the Engineering Council in the UK, and ABET accredits US programmes.
State boards license engineers in the United States; requirements vary by state.
Check your own country’s current registration, accreditation and CPD requirements with the official body.

en.title: Advanced manufacturing processes and precision engineering
en.short: Micro and nano processes, precision machine design, error budgets, process modelling and material selection.

sections.heading: Micro and nano manufacturing
sections.text:
Advanced manufacturing uses controlled, high-value processes rather than only conventional cutting and forming. Micro manufacturing makes parts or features roughly between 1 µm and 1 mm; nano manufacturing works below about 100 nm. At these scales surface forces, grain structure and tool edge radius matter more than bulk strength.

Examples include micro-milling, micro-electrical discharge machining (micro-EDM), lithography, nanoimprint lithography and scanning probe methods.

sections.heading: Precision machine design
sections.text:
Precision is the closeness of repeated results; accuracy is closeness to the true value; resolution is the smallest readable increment. A precision machine separates the metrology frame from the force frame, follows the Abbe principle (the measured length and the measuring scale must lie on the same line) and controls thermal growth.
